title: Off Campus Drive: How It Actually Works for Freshers in India
h1: Off Campus Drive: How It Actually Works for Freshers in India
seo_title: Off Campus Drive Guide for Indian Freshers (2026)
seo_description: How an off campus drive actually works in India — companies, eligibility, timelines, and what to do with no placement cell. Register for one today.
excerpt: Off-campus drives, not campus placement, are how most Indian freshers actually get hired. Here's how they work, who runs them, and what to do without a placement cell.
content_html:
An off campus drive is a hiring process a company runs independently of any specific college — anyone from an eligible batch and degree can apply, register, and sit for the assessment, regardless of which institution they studied at. This is different from on-campus placement, where only students of colleges the company has chosen to visit get access. In India, off-campus drives are how the majority of freshers actually get hired: TCS's NQT, Infosys's SE/DSE/PP tracks, Wipro, Cognizant, HCLTech, Accenture, and Capgemini all run recurring off-campus hiring cycles through the year, open to 2024, 2025, and 2026 batch graduates. If your college has a placement cell, off-campus is your backup. If it doesn't, off-campus is your primary route — and it works exactly as well.

On-campus vs off-campus: how the calendar actually works

On-campus placement in India runs on a fixed academic calendar. Most engineering and MBA colleges hold their placement season from roughly August to December, with a smaller second window in January–March for companies that didn't fill their quota in the first pass. Off-campus drives don't follow this calendar at all — companies run them whenever they have hiring need, which for large IT services firms is often multiple times a year.

On-campus placementAug–Dec (main season), Jan–Mar (second window)Only students of colleges the company visits

Product/startup off-campus hiringMostly rolling, spikes around fiscal year planning (Apr, Oct)Applicants who clear DSA/technical screens, college-agnostic

The practical implication: if you wait for campus season to end before trying off-campus routes, you've lost months. Register for off-campus drives the moment you're eligible, run them in parallel with campus applications, and don't treat one as a fallback for the other.

Companies that run regular off-campus drives

A handful of large IT services companies form the backbone of off-campus fresher hiring in India by sheer volume, running structured, recurring drives with defined tracks and salary bands. Accenture2025–2026 batches, ≥65%~4.5–6.5
Capgemini2025–2026 batches~3.8–6.0

Beyond IT services, product companies and GCCs (Global Capability Centres of companies like Microsoft, Google, and Amazon) also hire off-campus, but selectively and with a much heavier emphasis on data structures, algorithms, and system design rounds rather than a general aptitude test. These pay considerably more — often ₹15–40+ LPA reported for select 2026 fresher hires at product firms — but the funnel is far narrower. Treat IT services drives as your floor and product-company applications as your upside, not the other way around.

Eligibility patterns you'll see across almost every drive

Once you've looked at five or six off-campus drive postings, the pattern becomes obvious. Most companies use some version of the same filters:

  • Batch year window: Usually the current year plus the previous one or two (so in 2026, that's typically 2024, 2025, and 2026 pass-outs).
  • Minimum aggregate percentage: Commonly 60% throughout X, XII, and degree, sometimes stated as a 6.0/10 CGPA equivalent. A few companies (mostly product firms) don't filter on this at all and go straight to a skills test.
  • No active backlogs at the time of joining: Almost universal — you can usually apply with a pending backlog but must clear it before onboarding.
  • Degree/stream preference: Core IT/CSE/ECE streams get preference for technical tracks; some companies (HCLTech, certain BPO-style roles) accept any degree.
  • Gap year tolerance: Varies by company — some allow up to a 2-year education gap, others are stricter. Check the specific drive's notification rather than assuming.

None of these are negotiable at the application stage — the online system filters you out automatically if you don't meet them, so there's no point in applying and hoping. If your CGPA is on the border, apply to more drives rather than trying to argue your case for one.

Where to actually find off-campus drive announcements

This is the part most freshers get wrong — they wait for someone to send them a link instead of building a habit of checking.

  • Official career/registration portals: TCS uses nextstep.tcsapps.com; Infosys hires through its own careers site and InfyTQ platform. Bookmark these directly rather than relying on aggregators.
  • Naukri Campus and LinkedIn job alerts: Set alerts filtered to your batch year and role. For a full comparison of which portals are worth the time, see our guide to the best job portals in India.
  • Government portal ncs.gov.in: The National Career Service portal lists public-sector and PSU openings that many freshers never check.
  • Company LinkedIn and Twitter/X pages: Off-campus drive announcements often go out here before they're indexed by job portals.
  • WhatsApp/Telegram placement groups: Useful for speed, but treat every link with suspicion — see the red flags section below before you click "apply" on anything shared this way.

No placement cell? Here's what actually works

If your college doesn't run a placement process — common at many tier-2 and tier-3 colleges — you are not at a structural disadvantage for off-campus hiring, because off-campus drives don't check which college ran your process. What you lose is the coordination a placement cell would normally handle, so you have to replace it yourself.

  • Register directly. Go to nextstep.tcsapps.com, the Infosys careers page, and similar portals yourself. No college login or endorsement is needed for these drives.
  • Form a small group with classmates. Two or three people tracking drives together and sharing deadlines catches openings that one person alone will miss.
  • Use seniors as your informal placement cell. Batches that graduated one or two years before you are the best source of "here's what actually happened when I applied" information — reach out on LinkedIn.
  • Build the proof-of-work a placement cell can't give you. Without a college brand backing your resume, a project, an internship, or a certification does more work. Pair this with a properly built plan for getting a job as a fresher rather than applying at random.
  • Know your numbers before you accept anything. Once an offer comes in, run the CTC through an in-hand salary calculator before comparing offers — the headline LPA figure and what actually lands in your account monthly can differ by a wide margin once PF, professional tax, and other deductions are factored in.

Red flags: fake off-campus drives

Off-campus hiring's biggest weakness is that it's easy to impersonate. Naukri's own security centre lists the common pattern: a posting promises guaranteed selection or unusually high pay for a fresher role, asks for a "registration" or "processing" fee, and pushes for quick payment before any real interview happens. No legitimate company — TCS, Infosys, or any GCC — will ever ask you to pay to register for a drive or to receive an offer letter. If a WhatsApp forward links to a page asking for money before an assessment, assume it's fake and verify directly on the company's official career page instead.

What the process looks like once you register

Most IT services off-campus drives follow the same rough sequence, whether it's TCS, Infosys, or Wipro. Knowing the stages ahead of time means you're not caught off guard by a test you didn't prepare for.

  1. Online registration: You fill in your academic details, upload your resume, and select a test slot. This is also where the automatic eligibility filter (percentage, batch year, backlog status) applies.
  2. Aptitude/coding assessment: A proctored online test covering quantitative aptitude, logical reasoning, verbal ability, and — for technical tracks — basic coding. TCS NQT and Infosys's assessments both follow this pattern, though the coding weight is higher for Digital/DSE/PP tracks than for the entry-level Ninja/SE track.
  3. Technical interview: Covers your core subjects, projects, and sometimes a live coding problem. Product companies weight this stage far more heavily than IT services firms do.
  4. HR/managerial round: Standard questions about your background, willingness to relocate, and salary expectations. Prepare answers to common HR interview questions rather than winging this stage — it trips up more candidates than people expect.
  5. Offer and onboarding: Once selected, you'll get a formal offer letter with your CTC breakup. Read it fully before signing — bond clauses, notice period terms, and joining bonuses (if any) are all in there.

The full cycle from registration to offer typically takes anywhere from 3 weeks (fast-moving IT services drives) to 2–3 months (product companies with multiple technical rounds). Apply early in a cycle rather than at the deadline — slots for the assessment can fill up, and later batches sometimes face a higher effective cutoff simply because more seats have already been given away.

Frequently asked questions

What's the actual difference between on-campus and off-campus placement? On-campus is limited to students of colleges a company chooses to visit. Off-campus drives are open to any eligible graduate from the specified batch years, regardless of college, and typically run through the company's own portal rather than through your institution.

Can final-year students apply to off-campus drives before graduating? Yes, most drives explicitly include the upcoming graduating batch alongside the previous one or two years, since companies plan onboarding around expected graduation dates.

How many off-campus drives should I actually apply to? As many as you're eligible for. There's no penalty for applying to TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant, and others simultaneously — treat it as building parallel pipelines, not choosing one company to bet on.

Do off-campus drives pay less than on-campus offers? Not inherently — the same company often uses the same salary bands for both. What differs is competition volume and screening intensity, since off-campus drives draw applicants from across the country rather than one college's batch.

My college has no placement cell — am I disqualified from these drives? No. Off-campus drives are designed for exactly this situation. You register and apply directly with the company; your college's placement infrastructure (or lack of it) has no bearing on eligibility.

How do I know if an off-campus drive announcement is genuine? Cross-check it against the company's own official careers page or verified registration portal (for example, TCS's nextstep.tcsapps.com). If a listing asks for payment at any stage before an offer, it's not genuine — report and avoid it.

title: LinkedIn Profile Optimization for Freshers in India
h1: LinkedIn Profile Optimization for Freshers in India
seo_title: LinkedIn Profile Optimization for Freshers (2026 Guide)
seo_description: A step-by-step linkedin profile optimization checklist for Indian freshers covering photo, headline, About, skills, and search. Fix your profile this week.
excerpt: A section-by-section linkedin profile optimization checklist for Indian freshers, ordered by how much search weight each field actually carries.
content_html:
LinkedIn profile optimization for a fresher means making sure every field a recruiter's search actually reads — your photo, headline, About section, experience, and skills — carries the exact keywords for the role you want, in the order LinkedIn weighs them. It is not about adding more sections. A profile with a sharp photo, a keyword-led headline, a specific About section, 2–3 well-written experience entries, and 15–20 accurate skills will outperform a "complete" profile stuffed with generic filler every time. This guide walks through each section in the order it matters, with the specific fixes that move a fresher profile from invisible to found.

Start With What LinkedIn Search Actually Reads

Before touching any single section, understand how LinkedIn Recruiter search treats your profile. Analyses of LinkedIn's search behaviour consistently find that your name, headline, current job title and company, and skills section carry the highest keyword weight. Your About section, past roles, and education carry moderate weight. Recommendations and post content aren't indexed for profile search at all. That ranking should decide where you spend your effort first: headline and skills before you polish paragraph prose in About.

Practically, this means the same keyword should show up in more than one high-weight field. If you're targeting "Data Analyst" roles, that phrase (or close variants like "Business Analyst," "Analytics") should appear in your headline, your most recent experience title if applicable, and your skills list — not just buried once in a sentence in About.

The Optimization Checklist, Section by Section

SectionSearch weightWhat to fix first
PhotoIndirect (affects click-through, not search)Clear headshot, visible face, plain background, no filters, no graduation gown mid-shot with 12 other people cropped out
HeadlineHighest, after your nameRole + skill + proof point, front-loaded in the first 60–70 characters
Current position fieldHighList your most relevant internship, project role, or "Actively Seeking [Role]" if you have no title to add
SkillsHigh15–20 skills, ranked with your top 3 pinned, matching the exact words used in job postings you're targeting
About sectionModerateFront-load your target role and key skills in the first 2–3 lines, before the "See more" cutoff
Experience/ProjectsModerateEach entry gets 2–3 bullet points with a tool or metric, not a one-line job description
LocationModerateSet to the city you're actually job-hunting in, not your hometown if you've moved
Featured sectionNone (not indexed for search)Still worth using to pin a certificate, project link, or resume for anyone who opens your profile

Headline: Fix This Before Anything Else

Your headline is the second-highest-weight keyword field on your entire profile, right after your name. A generic headline like "Student at Delhi University" wastes that weight completely. Use the formula: role you're targeting, 2–3 relevant skills, one proof point (college, project, internship, certification), in that order, front-loaded because only around 60–70 characters of your 220-character allowance show up in search results and on mobile before truncation. For the full formula, situational templates, and common mistakes, see linkedin headline for freshers.

About Section: Write for the First Three Lines

LinkedIn's About field allows up to 2,600 characters, but only around the first 300 characters show before a reader has to click "See more." Most freshers waste that visible stretch on a throat-clearing opening line like "I am a passionate and dedicated individual." Rewrite it so the first three lines answer: who are you, what do you do or want to do, and what's your strongest proof point. Everything after the fold can go deeper — projects, tools, what you're looking for next.

For full About sections you can adapt directly, across engineering, commerce, marketing, and non-tech branches, see linkedin about section examples.

Skills, Experience, and the Fields Freshers Skip

Two sections freshers consistently under-invest in:

  • Skills. LinkedIn lets you list up to 50 skills, and you can pin your top 3 to display first. List the specific tools and languages from job postings you're targeting — "Advanced Excel," "Power BI," "Python," "SQL" — not vague categories like "Analytical Skills." Ask 2–3 people who know your work to endorse your top skills; endorsed skills read as more credible to anyone reviewing the profile manually, even though endorsements themselves aren't a search-ranking factor.
  • Experience and projects. Every internship, part-time role, or major college project deserves its own entry with 2–3 bullet points, each naming a tool and an outcome ("Built a inventory tracker in Python and MySQL, used by 3 college club events to track 200+ registrations") rather than a one-line description. If you genuinely have none of these yet, add a "Projects" entry for coursework or a hackathon — an empty experience section reads as an incomplete profile to anyone scanning it.

Freshers with zero internships often assume there's nothing to add here. There usually is: a college fest you helped organise, a paper you co-authored, a freelance gig, a certification project from Coursera or Google. Anything with a deliverable counts.

Photo, Banner, and the Fields That Affect Click-Through, Not Search

Your photo doesn't get indexed for keyword search, but it strongly affects whether a recruiter who found you clicks through or scrolls past. Profiles without a photo read as inactive or fake to many recruiters and get skipped by default. Use a recent, clear headshot with your face visible and good lighting — a phone photo against a plain wall works better than a blurry group photo from a farewell event. A custom banner image with your target role or a relevant line (many freshers use a simple "Open to [Role] Opportunities" banner) is optional polish, not a ranking factor.

Why This Matters More Right Now

Fresher hiring in India isn't uniform, and LinkedIn's role in it is growing. Naukri's JobSpeak report for January 2026 showed overall fresher hiring up 8% year-on-year, with non-IT sectors moving faster than tech — real estate fresher hiring up 42%, BPO/ITES up 39%, insurance up 35%, and hospitality up 33% over the same period, alongside steady healthcare fresher demand. That spread of demand across sectors means a well-optimized profile matters whether you're targeting an SDE role or an insurance sales trainee position — the fields that get you found in search are the same either way.

At the same time, more recruiters at Indian companies run their first candidate search directly inside LinkedIn Recruiter rather than opening a stack of resumes from Naukri or a campus placement portal, because it lets them filter by skill, title, and location in a single query. If your profile isn't optimized for that search, you're excluded from that first pass entirely, regardless of how strong your actual resume is. Pair your LinkedIn optimization with a resume that passes automated screening — see what is a good ATS score for how that separate filter works, since recruiters usually check both.

Recommendations, Endorsements, and the Fields That Don't Move Search but Still Matter

A few sections don't carry search weight but still influence whether a recruiter who opens your profile trusts what they see:

  • Recommendations. One or two written recommendations from a professor, internship manager, or team lead you worked under add credibility that endorsements can't — ask specifically, and give the person two lines about what you'd like them to mention (a project, a deadline you handled, a specific skill) rather than leaving it open-ended.
  • Education section. List your college, degree, and graduation year precisely, and add relevant coursework or a CGPA if it's strong — recruiters at campus-hiring-heavy companies do check this field even though it's not a primary search driver.
  • Certifications. Add certifications with the issuing platform's exact name (Google Data Analytics, NPTEL, Coursera Meta Front-End) rather than a generic description — some of these terms do get searched.
  • Activity and posts. Commenting thoughtfully on posts in your target field or sharing a project write-up keeps your profile from looking dormant, even though post content itself isn't indexed for profile search.

None of these substitute for fixing your headline, About, and skills first. But once those are done, a recommendation or two and an active-looking feed are what convert a profile view into an actual message from a recruiter.

A Common Trap: Optimizing for Completeness Instead of Search

LinkedIn shows you a "profile strength" indicator that nudges you to add more sections — volunteer experience, courses, languages, honours. Filling all of these does not meaningfully change your search visibility, because most of them sit outside the high-weight fields discussed above. A fresher who spends an evening filling in "Languages: Hindi, English" and skips rewriting a generic headline has optimized for the wrong thing. If you're short on time, the order of priority is: headline, then current position field, then skills, then About, then experience/projects. Everything else is polish you add once those five are solid.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does LinkedIn profile optimization take for a fresher?

Doing it properly — headline, About, skills, and 2–3 experience entries — takes about 2–3 hours in one sitting if you have your projects and internships listed somewhere already. Spread over a week if you're gathering project details or waiting on endorsements, but don't let it drag longer; a half-finished profile update looks worse than the original.

Does having a LinkedIn Premium or Open to Work badge affect search ranking?

The green "Open to Work" frame around your photo is a visibility signal to recruiters browsing, not a keyword-search ranking factor. Premium subscriptions unlock features like InMail and applicant insights but don't directly boost how your profile ranks in a recruiter's keyword search.

How many connections should a fresher have before job hunting seriously?

There's no magic number, but under 50 connections reads as a barely-used account to a recruiter checking your profile. Aim for 150–300 relevant connections — classmates, seniors, alumni, people at companies you're targeting — built genuinely rather than through mass connection requests.

Should freshers use LinkedIn or Naukri as the primary job search tool?

They serve different jobs. Naukri is built around applying to listed openings; LinkedIn is built around being found through search and networking, and increasingly around recruiters reaching out first. Most serious fresher job searches need both, plus campus and off-campus channels. See best job portals in India for how to split your effort.

Do I need a custom LinkedIn URL?

It's a small polish item, not a ranking factor. A custom URL like linkedin.com/in/yourname looks cleaner on a resume or email signature than the default string of numbers, and takes under a minute to set in your profile settings.

What's the single highest-impact change a fresher can make to their LinkedIn profile?

Rewriting the headline. It's the highest-weight keyword field after your name, it's visible everywhere your profile shows up (search results, comments, connection requests), and most freshers leave it at LinkedIn's generic default. Nothing else on the profile has that combination of high search weight and near-zero time cost to fix.

title: Topmate Alternative: Comparing Topmate, ADPList, Preplaced, and More
h1: Topmate Alternative: An Honest 2026 Comparison
seo_title: Topmate Alternative: Honest 2026 Comparison
seo_description: Weighing a topmate alternative? Compare Topmate, ADPList, Preplaced, MentorCruise, and GrowthMentor on cost and fit, then pick the right one.
excerpt: An honest, fairness-first comparison of Topmate against ADPList, Preplaced, MentorCruise, and GrowthMentor — cost, structure, and where each one is genuinely the better choice.
content_html:
If you're looking for a Topmate alternative, the honest answer is that Topmate is genuinely good at what it's built for — a wide, searchable marketplace of experts across careers, astrology, fitness, and everything else, with mentors setting their own prices and Topmate taking a platform commission (commonly cited around 10%, though effective costs run higher on international payments once gateway and conversion fees are added). Whether an alternative is actually "better" depends entirely on what you need: free one-off advice, structured India-specific long-term mentorship, a global subscription mentor, or startup-founder-specific guidance. This piece compares Topmate against ADPList, Preplaced, MentorCruise, and GrowthMentor on cost, structure, and fit, and is honest about where each one — including Topmate — is the right call.

Quick comparison

PlatformTypical costBest forWhere it falls short
TopmateMentor-set, typically ₹500-₹7,500+ per session; ~10% platform commissionWidest range of experts across career, tech, and non-career fields; one-off sessionsQuality and depth vary widely by mentor since anyone can list; no built-in vetting for career-specific expertise
ADPListFree for menteesA first free conversation, resume or mock-interview review, quick outside perspectiveNo continuity — booking the same mentor twice is hard; mentor availability is inconsistent
PreplacedPersonalized, often ~₹5,000-₹7,500+/month per mentor (mentor-set); 5% student discount; 7-day money-back guaranteeIndia-specific, longer-term 1:1 mentorship with mentors from MAANG/large product companies, referralsCost is a real commitment upfront; value depends heavily on the individual mentor match
MentorCruise$50-$800+/month subscription; ~16.6% average platform feeGlobal mentor pool, structured monthly plans with ongoing chat accessPriced in USD, which is expensive relative to Indian salaries; fewer mentors with India-specific context
GrowthMentor$49/mo (Light) or $99/mo (Pro)Startup founders and growth/marketing professionalsNot built for students or freshers — the mentor pool and content skew toward founders, not campus-to-corporate transitions
CheatcodeNot yet public — early access waitlistFinal-year students and 0-2 YOE professionals specifically, matched to mentors with 5-10+ years of relevant experienceNot live yet — you can join the waitlist at cheatcodeapp.com but can't book a session today

Topmate: what it does well, and where it doesn't

Topmate's real strength is breadth and speed. With reportedly over 1 million professionals having used the platform and 100,000+ reviews, it's one of the largest marketplaces of its kind serving India, and you can book a session with almost anyone — a specific ex-Amazon PM, a UX portfolio reviewer, a specific YouTuber — within minutes. For a narrow, one-time need where you already know exactly who you want to talk to, that's genuinely hard to beat.

The tradeoff is that Topmate is a marketplace, not a curated mentorship program — anyone can list a profile and set a price, so quality and depth vary a lot between mentors, and there's limited structure connecting one session to the next. A guide on Topmate's own fee structure noted that the bottom 80% of creators on the platform earn less than ₹5,000 a month, which is a useful signal that the bulk of activity is small, one-off sessions rather than deep, sustained mentoring relationships. If you need a single sharp answer, that's fine. If you need someone checking in with you over months, it's not really what the platform is built for.

ADPList: honestly, hard to beat on price

ADPList's pitch — "free forever," no paywalls — is real, not a loss-leader gimmick. It lists more than 40,000 verified mentors across design, product, engineering, AI, and marketing, and every session is free for the mentee. For a student who just wants a second opinion on a resume, a mock interview, or a quick sanity check on an offer, ADPList is very likely the best possible first stop, and it's the one we'd recommend trying before spending any money elsewhere.

Where it's weaker: the free model means popular mentors get booked out fast, and there's no mechanism for ongoing continuity with the same person — you're essentially getting one good conversation, not a relationship. It's also global by design, so India-specific context (CTC structures, notice period norms, campus placement timelines) isn't guaranteed from any given mentor.

Preplaced: the strongest India-specific option for depth

Preplaced is built specifically for the Indian market and leans into long-term mentorship rather than one-off calls — unlimited chat access with an assigned mentor, task-based structure, and referral support through the mentor's own network, with mentors drawn from MAANG and other large product companies. It also offers a 100% money-back guarantee within 7 days and a mentor-change policy if the initial match isn't working, both of which meaningfully de-risk paying upfront. It's worth taking seriously if your goal is a structured, multi-week push toward a specific transition, like a service-to-product switch.

The fair caveat: pricing is set per mentor and isn't published as a flat rate, so you won't know the exact cost until a trial conversation, and — like any 1:1 marketplace — outcomes depend heavily on which specific mentor you're matched with, not just the platform's process.

MentorCruise: solid if you want a global mentor and can pay in dollars

MentorCruise runs on monthly subscriptions to individual mentors, with plans documented from under $50 to $800+ a month, plus one-off session options in the $9-$39 range. The platform takes roughly a 16.6% average commission, layered into the mentee's price rather than charged separately. Its strength is a genuinely global, experienced mentor pool with a clear subscription structure — you know exactly what you're paying monthly and what's included.

For Indian students and freshers specifically, the honest limitation is currency and context: prices in USD translate to a meaningful chunk of an entry-level Indian salary, and the mentor pool, while strong globally, has fewer people with direct experience of Indian company structures, notice periods, or campus-to-corporate timelines.

GrowthMentor: excellent, but not for this audience

It would be unfair to ding GrowthMentor for not being what it doesn't claim to be. At $49/month (Light) or $99/month (Pro) for unlimited calls, it's a strong, well-reviewed platform — but it's built for startup founders and growth/marketing professionals working on business problems, not for students or freshers navigating placements, first jobs, or early-career switches. If you're a fresher who's also bootstrapping a side project or startup, it could be a genuinely useful complement. As a primary mentorship platform for a final-year student, it's the wrong tool for the job, and would be misleading to recommend as one.

Where Cheatcode fits, honestly

Cheatcode is built specifically for the audience this comparison is about — final-year students and professionals with 0-2 years of experience — matched with mentors who have 5-10+ years of relevant industry experience. It isn't live yet. There's an early-access waitlist at cheatcodeapp.com, and pricing and mentor availability aren't public. If the platforms above already solve your immediate need, use them — that's what they're for today. If you'd rather wait for something purpose-built for exactly this stage of career, the waitlist is where to start.

Questions to ask before paying any of these platforms

Regardless of which one you pick, a few questions upfront save you from a bad match after you've already paid. Ask the mentor directly: how many mentees are you currently working with (an overloaded mentor gives shallow attention regardless of platform), what does a typical month of support actually look like (calls, async chat, or both), and what happens if the fit isn't working — is there a refund window or a mentor-swap option. Preplaced publishes its 7-day guarantee and swap policy openly, which is a genuinely good practice; on marketplaces like Topmate or ADPList, you're often relying on the individual mentor's goodwill rather than a platform-wide policy, so ask directly instead of assuming.

It's also worth checking how recently the mentor was in a role similar to where you're headed. A mentor who switched from a service company to a product company eight years ago has less current information than one who did it eighteen months ago — hiring bars, interview formats, and CTC bands shift faster than most mentor bios reveal.

How to actually choose

  • Need one free opinion today: ADPList first, always.
  • Need a specific named person for a one-off session: Topmate's breadth wins here.
  • Want structured, India-specific, multi-week mentorship with referrals: Preplaced is the strongest fit, with the caveat that cost depends on your matched mentor.
  • Comfortable paying in USD for a global subscription mentor: MentorCruise.
  • Running a startup or side business alongside your job: GrowthMentor, as a supplement, not a replacement.

Whichever platform you pick, go in with a specific question rather than a general "help me with my career" ask — see our list of questions to ask a mentor for exact phrasing by situation, and our broader guide on how to find a mentor for free options to try before paying for any of the above.

Frequently asked questions

Is Topmate free for mentees? No — mentors set their own prices for sessions, and Topmate takes a platform commission on top, commonly cited around 10%, though international payments can add gateway and conversion costs.

title: Resume Maker for Freshers: The Honest 2026 Comparison
h1: Resume Maker for Freshers: Which One Actually Fits 0 Experience
seo_title: Resume Maker for Freshers: Best Free Options 2026
seo_description: A resume maker for freshers should fit one page and skip subscriptions. Compare Naukri360, FlowCV, Canva and Kickresume, then build yours for free today.
excerpt: Most resume makers are built for a ten-year career, not a fresher with two projects and an internship. Here's how Naukri360, FlowCV, Canva, Kickresume, Zety and Novoresume actually handle a fresher's resume — and why paying for a subscription usually isn't the right first move.
content_html:
If you're a final-year student or a fresher with zero to two years of experience, a resume maker for freshers needs to do three things a general resume builder doesn't always get right: default to one page, treat a "Projects" and "Internships" section as seriously as "Work Experience," and not lock the PDF behind a subscription you can't justify on a student budget. Most international tools — Zety, Novoresume, Resume.io — were designed around a career-changer with ten years of work history, not someone with two college projects and a three-month internship. Naukri360 and FlowCV's free tier handle the fresher case better because their default templates fit a short resume without making it look empty. Here's how the major resume makers actually handle a fresher's resume, and which one to open before your next campus or off-campus drive.

What a fresher's resume actually needs

A fresher's resume is a different document from a five-year professional's, not a shorter version of the same one. It needs to fit on a single page, lead with Education and Projects rather than a thin Experience section, and use a headline that states the target role clearly since there's no job title history to imply it. A resume maker built around long "Work Experience" blocks will leave a fresher's page looking sparse, which pushes some people toward decorative templates to fill the space — exactly the wrong instinct, since decorative usually means less ATS-safe. This article is specifically about which tool to build it in; the content and structure decisions — what to put in a headline, how to describe a project with no real "results" yet, what to do about a low CGPA — are a separate problem covered in our resume format for freshers guide.

There's a timing element too, specific to India. Most engineering and MBA campuses run their placement season roughly from August to December, with a second wave of off-campus and pooled drives running from January through June for students who didn't get placed in the first round. A resume maker that takes you twenty minutes to set up matters more in the first scenario, when a TPO announces a drive with two days' notice, than in the second, when you have more time to be deliberate about which tool and which template you use.

The fresher-specific problem every generic resume maker has

Open Zety, Novoresume, or Resume.io and start a new resume, and the default flow assumes you have at least one job to list. The "Work Experience" section sits at the top, sized for multiple entries with dates, promotions, and responsibilities. A fresher with one three-month internship fills that section in two lines and is left staring at a page that's two-thirds empty — which is precisely the moment a lot of people reach for a busier, more decorative template to make the page look fuller. That instinct is understandable and almost always the wrong call, because a template with icons, a sidebar, or a photo header is also the template most likely to confuse an ATS parser used by a larger recruiter. Naukri360 and FlowCV's default templates handle this better simply because they don't over-allocate space to a section freshers don't have much to fill, and they let Projects and Education carry the page instead.

There's also a currency-and-commitment mismatch worth naming directly. A final-year student, by definition, has no income yet. Being asked to pay $21.99/month for Novoresume or start a $1.95 trial that renews at $25.95 every four weeks on Zety is a genuinely different proposition for a student than for someone already earning a salary. None of these tools price for that difference — the same subscription costs the same whether you're a fresher building your first resume or a five-year professional negotiating a jump to 18 LPA.

Resume maker comparison for freshers (checked August 2026)

ZetyBuild onlyNo, TXT export onlyYes, but paywalled$1.95/14-day trial, then $25.95/4 weeks
Novoresume1-page Basic templateNo, once Premium touchedYes, on Basic template$21.99/month

Free options that fit a student's budget

Naukri360 is the default recommendation for most freshers doing campus or off-campus applications in India. It's free, it exports both PDF and Word, and because Naukri is where a huge share of Indian recruiters actually search for candidates, using its own resume builder means your formatting is already consistent with how its resume database (RESDEX) reads profiles. FlowCV is the second-best free option, particularly if you want a slightly more modern-looking template than Naukri360 offers — you just get one saved resume on the free tier, which is fine if you're applying to a fairly narrow set of role types.

Avoid the instinct to reach for a paid subscription resume builder as a fresher. With one job title's worth of content, projects, and an internship or two, there's very little a ₹1,800/month tool gives you that a free single-column template doesn't — the content and the keyword match to the job description matter far more than the design.

When a paid tool is actually worth it for a fresher

The one case where paying makes some sense: if you're running a high-volume off-campus job search and applying to genuinely different role types — say, both software engineering and data analyst roles — and you want several distinct, well-organised resume versions live at once without manually duplicating documents. Kickresume's cheapest yearly plan (around $6.40/month, billed in USD) or FlowCV's paid tier cover that case reasonably. Even then, the resume tool is a small part of the equation; how quickly you can get a decent resume in front of enough recruiters usually matters more than which builder you used to make it.

It's also worth being realistic about what "high volume" means for a fresher in India. If you're sending out 30–40 applications a week during peak placement season, a single well-tailored resume with two or three variants is usually enough. Most freshers overestimate how many distinct resume versions they actually need and underestimate how much a slightly-off headline or missing keyword costs them per application.

Mistakes a resume maker won't catch for you

No tool on this list, free or paid, stops you from making the mistakes that actually sink most fresher resumes. A builder checks that your sections exist and your formatting is consistent; it has no opinion on whether the content inside those sections is any good. These are the ones we see most often:

  • Writing an "Objective" instead of a headline. "Seeking an opportunity to utilise my skills" wastes the first line every recruiter reads. See our resume headline for freshers guide for what to write instead.
  • Listing projects without outcomes. "Built a to-do app in React" tells a recruiter nothing about scope. What did it do, who used it, what was the result, and what specific technologies did you actually touch?
  • Copying a two-column Canva template because it looks more "designed" — most ATS instances used by large Indian employers still struggle with multi-column layouts, and a fresher has the least room to gamble on a template choice they haven't tested.
  • Forgetting to match the exact job title from the posting in your headline and summary, which is one of the strongest single ranking signals in keyword-based recruiter search, and one of the easiest to fix in under a minute per application.
  • Sending the same unedited resume to every application during placement season instead of adjusting the top third for each specific role.
  • Including irrelevant personal details — father's name, marital status, a photo — that were common on older Indian resume formats but add nothing to how a modern ATS or recruiter evaluates you, and can occasionally work against you.

How much time this should actually take

A fresher building a first resume from scratch on Naukri360 or FlowCV's free tier should expect roughly 30–45 minutes if the content — projects, internship details, skills, education — is already organised beforehand. Most of the time people spend "stuck" on a resume builder isn't spent fighting the tool; it's spent trying to figure out what to actually write in the Projects section, which is a content problem, not a tool problem. Sorting out your bullet points in a plain document first, then pasting them into whichever builder you've picked, is almost always faster than trying to write and format at the same time inside the tool's editor.

What this looks like across a real placement season

Most engineering colleges in India schedule their main campus placement window between August and December, with companies visiting on specific dates coordinated through the TPO. A student going through this season typically needs one strong base resume, tailored in small ways — headline, top skills, sometimes the order of projects — for each visiting company's stated role. This is a very different use case from someone doing an unstructured off-campus search across dozens of unrelated postings on Naukri or LinkedIn between January and June, who benefits more from having two or three genuinely distinct resume versions ready rather than one resume with minor tweaks. Knowing which situation you're in changes whether a single free resume slot (FlowCV) is enough or whether you actually need Naukri360's unlimited free resumes to keep multiple versions live at once.

One more India-specific point worth flagging: a large share of placement cells now explicitly ask students to also upload or link a Naukri profile alongside the PDF resume, since many companies pull directly from Naukri's own applicant pool for follow-up drives. Keeping your Naukri360 resume and your Naukri profile headline in sync avoids a mismatch that a sharp recruiter will notice.

What we'd actually recommend

For a fresher building a first resume right now, open Naukri360 or FlowCV's free tier, not a paid subscription tool. Get the content and structure right first, then check it against the actual job description you're applying to — matching the posting's exact wording for your target job title and skills matters more than any template choice. If you later find you're applying to several distinct role types at volume, that's the point to consider a paid tool — our full best resume builder in India comparison covers which paid option is worth it and which isn't, and it's worth reading before you subscribe to anything.

Frequently asked questions

faq.q: Which resume maker is best for freshers with no experience?
faq.a: Naukri360 or FlowCV's free tier. Both default to a one-page, single-column format that fits a fresher's Projects-and-Education-led content without needing a paid subscription.

faq.q: Do I need to pay for a resume maker before campus placements?
faq.a: No. Most TPO-driven campus placements care about a clean, correctly formatted PDF with your projects, CGPA, and skills clearly listed — not the design. A free tool covers this completely.

faq.q: How long should a fresher's resume be?
faq.a: One page. With limited work history, projects, internships, education, and skills, a fresher's content almost always fits on a single page — stretching it to two pages usually means padding, not more substance.

faq.q: Can I use Canva for a campus placement resume?
faq.a: Yes, but pick a plain single-column template. Many of Canva's most popular resume designs use icons, colour blocks, or two-column layouts that can cause parsing issues in the ATS instances some larger recruiters use.

faq.q: What if my college placement cell asks for a specific format?
faq.a: Follow that format exactly, even if it looks plainer than a builder template. TPO-shared formats are usually already tuned to whatever the visiting company's application system expects.

faq.q: Is Naukri360 good enough for off-campus applications too, not just campus ones?
faq.a: Yes. Off-campus applications go through public postings on Naukri, LinkedIn, or company career pages that often run on Workday or Taleo — a plain, single-column Naukri360 export parses cleanly on those too.

title: Software Engineer Resume Format: Section Order, Skills, and a Full Example
h1: Software Engineer Resume Format: Section Order, Skills, and a Full Example
seo_title: Software Engineer Resume Format (India, 2026 Guide)
seo_description: Follow this software engineer resume format to pass TCS, Infosys, and product-company screens in India — use the worked example and build yours now.
excerpt: The exact software engineer resume format Indian recruiters screen for, with a categorized skills breakdown, project rewrites, and a full worked resume example.
content_html:
The software engineer resume format that clears Indian screening rounds is one page, with a Skills section (languages, DSA, frameworks, tools) placed right after Education, followed by 2-4 projects that each name real tools and a measurable result — not a list of tutorials. Service companies like TCS and Infosys screen mainly for CGPA cutoffs, no active backlogs, and basic coding-test scores; product companies and startups screen for DSA depth, project complexity, and GitHub activity. Both want to see a coding profile (LeetCode, Codeforces, or GeeksforGeeks) or a GitHub link somewhere visible, and neither wants a resume padded with every language and framework you've touched once. Below is the exact section order, what to actually put in Skills and Projects, a full worked resume example, and the mistakes specific to software engineer resumes.

What Indian recruiters screen for, and it's not the same for every company

The screening bar and the screening method both change depending on who's hiring.

Recruiter typeWhat they scan for firstTypical screening method
IT services (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant)CGPA cutoff (usually 60-65%), no active backlogs, basic DSA and aptitudeNQT/AMCAT/CoCubes-style aptitude + coding test, then HR round
Product companies and well-funded startupsDSA depth, project complexity, CS fundamentals, GitHub activityTake-home assignment or live coding round on HackerRank/Codility, then system-design-lite discussion
Off-campus mass drives via portalsResume keyword match against the JD, then coding test scoreNaukri/LinkedIn application into the company's own ATS, filtered before a human sees it

Reported 2026 CTC bands give a sense of what these tracks actually pay, so you can calibrate which ones are worth optimizing your resume for: TCS NQT runs Ninja (₹3.36-3.6 LPA), Digital (₹7-7.5 LPA), and Prime (up to ₹12.26 LPA) tracks based on cognitive score and interview performance; Infosys's off-campus tracks run Systems Engineer (₹3.6-4.5 LPA), Digital Specialist Engineer (₹6.5-9 LPA), and Power Programmer (₹8-12 LPA). These figures come from candidate-reported offers and 2026 placement-drive coverage rather than official company statements, but they're consistent enough across sources to plan around.

The exact section order for a software engineer resume

  1. Header — name, phone, email, city, LinkedIn, GitHub link
  2. Resume headline — role + degree + top skills; see our resume headline guide for freshers if you need the formula
  3. Education — degree, college, CGPA, year
  4. Skills — grouped by category, not a flat list
  5. Projects — 2-4, each with tools, what you built, and one measurable outcome
  6. Internship (if any) — company, duration, one concrete line on impact
  7. Certifications & Coding Profiles — LeetCode/Codeforces rating, relevant certs, hackathon results

Skills section: what to actually list

Group by category so it reads as a competency map, not a keyword dump.

  • Languages: pick a primary (Java, Python, or C++) and one secondary — listing six languages you've each used once signals breadth without depth.
  • Core CS fundamentals: Data Structures & Algorithms, Object-Oriented Programming, DBMS, Operating Systems, Computer Networks — these are exactly what service-company aptitude rounds and product-company phone screens both test.
  • Web/Backend: REST APIs, and one framework — Spring Boot (Java), Django/Flask (Python), or Node.js/Express (JavaScript) — plus a frontend basic like React if you've built anything full-stack.
  • Databases: MySQL or PostgreSQL, and MongoDB if you've used a NoSQL store in a project.
  • Tools: Git/GitHub, Postman, basic Docker, Linux command line — these come up in almost every technical interview as a quick "have you used this" check.

Projects section: how to describe them so they read as engineering, not tutorials

The single biggest gap between a fresher resume that gets shortlisted and one that doesn't is how projects are written. "Built a machine learning project" and "Built a to-do app" are both instantly forgettable because they could describe a 2-hour YouTube tutorial. Name the tools, the scale, and one number.

Weak versionRewritten with tools + outcome
Built an e-commerce websiteBuilt a 15-endpoint REST API (Java, Spring Boot, MySQL) for product catalog, cart, and orders with JWT auth; 40+ JUnit tests, deployed on Render
Made a chat appBuilt a real-time chat app (Node.js, Socket.io, MongoDB, React) handling 100+ concurrent WebSocket connections in local load tests; added Redis caching, cutting duplicate DB reads by ~40%
Did a machine learning projectTrained a Naive Bayes classifier (Python, scikit-learn) on a 10,000-row labeled news dataset, 87% test accuracy, exposed via a Flask API

Every rewritten version answers three questions in one line: what tools, how big/complex, and what happened when it ran. That's the template — apply it to whatever you've actually built.

Full worked example: a software engineer fresher resume

This is a complete, realistic resume using the format above. Copy the structure, not the specific projects — yours should reflect what you actually built.

Rohan Mehta

Bengaluru, Karnataka | rohan.mehta@email.com | +91-98xxxxxx10 | linkedin.com/in/rohanmehta | github.com/rohanmehta

Software Engineer Fresher | B.Tech CSE 2026 | Java, DSA, Spring Boot, React | 350+ LeetCode Problems Solved

Education

  • B.Tech, Computer Science and Engineering — XYZ Institute of Technology, Pune | CGPA: 8.4/10 | 2022-2026
  • Class XII (CBSE) — 89% | Class X (CBSE) — 91%

Skills

  • Languages: Java, Python, JavaScript
  • Core CS: Data Structures & Algorithms, OOP, DBMS, Operating Systems, Computer Networks
  • Web/Backend: Spring Boot, REST APIs, Node.js, Express.js, React.js
  • Databases: MySQL, MongoDB
  • Tools: Git, GitHub, Postman, Docker (basic), Linux

Projects

  • E-commerce REST API (Java, Spring Boot, MySQL) — Built a 15-endpoint REST API for product catalog, cart, and order flow with JWT authentication; wrote 40+ unit tests with JUnit achieving 85% code coverage; deployed on Render. (github.com/rohanmehta/ecommerce-api)
  • Real-Time Chat Application (Node.js, Socket.io, MongoDB, React) — Built a chat app handling 100+ concurrent WebSocket connections in local load testing; added Redis-based session caching to cut duplicate DB reads by ~40%; deployed frontend on Vercel, backend on Railway. (github.com/rohanmehta/chat-app)
  • Fake News Classifier (Python, scikit-learn, Flask) — Trained a Naive Bayes/logistic regression model on a 10,000-row labeled news dataset, reaching 87% test accuracy; exposed predictions through a Flask API with a minimal HTML frontend. (github.com/rohanmehta/fake-news-classifier)

Internship

Software Engineering Intern, [Startup Name], Pune — May 2025 to July 2025. Fixed 12 bugs and shipped 2 minor features in a Django-based internal tool used by 30+ employees; wrote migration scripts that cut a manual data-cleanup task from 3 hours to 10 minutes.

Certifications & Achievements

Solved 350+ problems on LeetCode (top 15% India rank on a recent contest) | Codeforces rating: 1350 (Pupil) | Winner, 24-hour hackathon, college tech fest, 2025 | AWS Cloud Practitioner Essentials (Coursera)

Coding profiles, GitHub, and certifications: what to include and what to skip

  • LeetCode/Codeforces/GeeksforGeeks: include a number only if it's genuinely worth mentioning (100+ problems, a contest rating). A low number framed honestly is fine too — just don't inflate it, since a live coding round will expose the gap immediately.
  • GitHub: pin your 3 best repositories with a proper README (what it does, how to run it, a screenshot if it has a UI). Forty empty or forked repos with no commits signal a profile built for appearance, not use.
  • Certifications: keep them role-relevant — AWS/GCP basics, a DSA course, a backend specialization. A generic "MS Office" or "Typing certificate" next to Spring Boot dilutes the technical signal you're trying to send.

Common mistakes specific to software engineer resumes

  1. Listing every language and framework you've touched once. A recruiter reading "Java, Python, C++, C, JavaScript, Go, Rust, PHP, Kotlin" assumes shallow exposure to all of them, not mastery of any.
  2. No live or deployed links, only GitHub source. A deployed link (Render, Vercel, Railway) that a recruiter can click and actually use takes your project from "claim" to "proof" in one click.
  3. A DSA-only resume with zero built projects. Fine for a pure service-company aptitude round, but product companies and most off-campus product-adjacent roles want to see something you shipped, not just problems you solved.
  4. Backlog history formatted inconsistently. If you cleared a backlog, don't leave stale semester gaps unexplained — a one-line note under Education is enough.
  5. Copy-pasted tutorial projects with no differentiation. "Tic Tac Toe," "Calculator," and "Netflix Clone" are the three most repeated fresher projects in India — if you built one, add a twist (multiplayer over WebSockets, a recommendation feature, a real dataset) or replace it with something more original.

What happens after your resume gets shortlisted

Getting past the resume screen is one filter, not the finish line. Service-company drives move straight into an aptitude-plus-coding test followed by a technical and HR round — if that's your track, look at real TCS interview questions or Infosys interview questions so you know what's actually asked before you walk in. Product-company and startup interviews tend to dig deeper into the exact projects on your resume — expect to explain your design choices, not just recite what's written, and run your resume once more through an ATS format check if you're applying through an online portal rather than a referral.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the ideal resume format for a software engineer fresher? One page, reverse-chronological, with Education followed immediately by a categorized Skills section and 2-4 projects that each name tools and a measurable outcome. See our broader resume format guide for freshers for the base structure this builds on.

How many projects should a fresher software engineer resume have? Two to four is the sweet spot. Fewer than two looks thin; more than four usually means some are weak and diluting the strong ones.

Should I include my LeetCode or Codeforces profile on my resume? Yes, if the number is decent (100+ solved, or a rated contest performance) — it's a fast proxy for DSA ability that both service and product companies use.

Do service companies like TCS and Infosys care about GitHub? Less than product companies do, but it doesn't hurt — their first filter is usually CGPA and an aptitude/coding test score, not your GitHub activity. Product companies weight it more heavily.

What CGPA cutoff do most Indian IT companies use? Many service companies apply a soft cutoff around 60-65% aggregate or equivalent CGPA for campus and off-campus drives, though this varies by company and hiring cycle — check the specific drive's eligibility criteria rather than assuming.

Should DSA and web development both appear on the resume, or should I pick one? Both, if you have them — DSA signals problem-solving ability for coding rounds, and a built project signals you can actually ship something end to end. Together they cover what service-company tests and product-company interviews each check for.

title: Notice Period Rules India: What Law Says vs Your Contract
h1: Notice Period Rules India: What Law Says vs Your Contract
seo_title: Notice Period Rules India: Law vs Your Contract Explained
seo_description: Notice period rules india explained: what law mandates, what contracts add, and buyout math. Check your numbers before you resign.
excerpt: Notice period rules in India come from two sources: a thin statutory baseline and a much bigger contractual layer. Here's what's actually enforceable, what buyouts cost, and where the law is genuinely unclear.
content_html:
Notice period rules india come from two different sources that often get confused: what the law actually mandates, and what your employment contract adds on top of that. For most salaried, white-collar employees (what labour law calls "non-workmen"), there's no single central law fixing 30, 60, or 90 days — that number comes from your contract. What law does provide is a baseline: state-level Shops and Establishments Acts generally require "reasonable notice" (commonly read as one month) before termination, and the Industrial Disputes Act mandates one month's notice or pay in lieu specifically for "workmen" — a legal category that doesn't cover most IT, managerial, or supervisory roles. Everything else — 60-day, 90-day clauses, buyout terms, forfeiture on resignation — is a matter of contract law, not a fixed statutory rule, and courts have shown limits on how far an employer can push it.

What Indian law actually mandates on notice period

Three sets of rules apply, depending on who you are:

  • Shops and Establishments Acts (state-level) — cover most commercial establishments and typically require "reasonable notice," which is usually interpreted as one month for permanent employees, though exact wording and enforcement varies by state.
  • Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 — applies specifically to "workmen" (a defined term covering manual, skilled, unskilled, and clerical work, but generally excluding managerial and supervisory roles). It mandates one month's notice or wages in lieu, plus retrenchment compensation of 15 days' average pay per year of service, for termination not amounting to punishment.
  • Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 — applies to larger factories and industrial establishments, where certified Standing Orders set out specific notice terms binding on both employer and employee.

For most people reading this — software engineers, analysts, marketers, product roles — none of these directly fix a number. Your notice period is whatever your appointment letter or contract says, subject to it being "reasonable" under general contract law.

Why contracts routinely ask for 30-90 days, and whether that's enforceable

Companies write long notice periods into contracts because they need time to find and train a replacement, especially for senior or specialised roles. Courts have generally upheld negotiated notice period clauses as reasonable business terms, not as a "restraint of trade" under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act — that section is more commonly invoked against post-employment non-compete clauses, not the notice period itself. That said, courts have pushed back on notice clauses that are wildly disproportionate to the role, or that operate one-sidedly (for example, a contract that lets the employer terminate you in 7 days but requires you to serve 90). If you're ever in that kind of dispute, treat this as a genuinely unsettled area — the outcome depends heavily on the specific facts, the state, and the forum, and this isn't a substitute for legal advice from someone who's reviewed your actual contract.

Notice period buyout: how it works and what it costs

A buyout — paying your current employer for the days of notice you don't serve — is legal as long as both sides agree to it, either through a clause already in your contract or through mutual consent at the time you resign. The standard calculation is: (gross monthly salary ÷ 30) × number of unserved days, deducted from your final settlement or paid upfront, depending on company policy. Some companies allow full buyout, some allow partial (say, serve 30 of your 60 days and buy out the rest), and some don't allow it at all and require full service. If your new employer is covering the buyout cost as a joining incentive, get that commitment in writing before you resign from your current job — verbal assurances during negotiation have a way of disappearing once you've already quit. This is exactly the kind of term worth raising while you still have leverage — see how to negotiate salary and other offer terms for how to ask for it.

Here's what the math actually looks like. Say your gross monthly salary is ₹90,000 and your contract requires 60 days' notice, but you can only serve 30 before your new employer needs you:

ItemCalculationAmount (₹)
Per-day salary90,000 ÷ 303,000
Unserved days60 − 3030 days
Buyout amount3,000 × 3090,000

That ₹90,000 is typically deducted from your final settlement or paid by you (or your new employer, if agreed) directly to your current company. It's calculated on gross salary, not CTC and not in-hand salary, so don't assume it'll match the number you see on your monthly payslip.

Relieving letter and full and final settlement: what's actually required

This is one of the murkiest areas in Indian employment practice. There's no single statute that explicitly mandates a "relieving letter" as a document — it's an industry convention that's become a de facto requirement for background checks and joining formalities at your next employer. Employers routinely tie its release to completion of your notice period, handover, and asset return, and while courts have said relieving letters "cannot be arbitrarily withheld once all obligations are fulfilled," enforcing that in practice usually means legal action, which most employees can't afford to pursue over a document. Treat this pragmatically: assume you need to complete your notice and handover cleanly to get one, rather than relying on a legal right that's genuinely unclear and slow to enforce.

Full and final settlement is on firmer legal ground. The Code on Wages (Central) Rules, 2020 requires full and final settlement — your pending salary, leave encashment, and other dues — to be paid within two working days of your last working day. In practice, many companies still take 30-45 days, and enforcement against delayed settlement is inconsistent. If your gratuity is part of that settlement, understand how it's calculated separately — see how gratuity is calculated in India — since it's often the line item companies take longest to process.

How notice period interacts with PSU, government, and contract roles

Government and PSU roles usually follow internal service rules rather than a standard private-sector contract — notice periods here often run 1-3 months and can involve additional formalities like a "No Objection Certificate" for lateral moves within government bodies. Fixed-term contract employees and consultants generally aren't bound by the same notice conventions as permanent employees, since the underlying relationship is a contract for service rather than a contract of employment — but check the specific termination clause in your contract rather than assuming shorter notice applies by default, since many contract roles now mirror permanent-employee notice terms exactly.

Notice period during probation, and what happens if you just leave

Most companies set a shorter notice period during probation — commonly 7-15 days — which reverts to the full contractual period once you're confirmed. If you resign without serving notice and without a buyout agreement, employers can legally withhold your relieving letter, deduct notice pay from your final settlement (up to the value of the unserved notice, not more), and in rare cases pursue a breach of contract claim, though that's uncommon for typical roles and modest amounts. It generally doesn't affect your PF or gratuity eligibility, which are governed by separate rules tied to service length, not how you exited.

Before you resign anywhere, know what your CTC actually converts to on both sides of the move — see CTC vs in-hand salary — and run the numbers on the in-hand salary calculator so a notice period buyout deduction doesn't come as a surprise on your last payslip.

Employment law varies by state and by the specific wording of your contract, and enforcement in practice often differs from what the statute technically allows. This article explains the general framework, not a legal opinion on your specific situation — for an actual dispute, consult a lawyer who can read your contract.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a maximum legal notice period in India?

No fixed statutory maximum applies to most white-collar roles — it's set by contract. Courts can strike down a clause as unreasonable in specific disputes, but there's no blanket number in law.

Can my employer refuse to relieve me even after my notice period ends?

Not legally, once your obligations (handover, dues, disciplinary matters) are cleared. In practice, delays happen, and pursuing it legally is often impractical for the amounts involved — most people resolve it by completing handover cleanly rather than through legal action.

Can I negotiate a shorter notice period after I've already signed the offer letter?

Yes, informally, especially if your new employer is willing to compensate for a buyout or wait a bit longer. It requires mutual agreement — you can't unilaterally shorten it.

Does notice period length affect my gratuity or PF?

No. Gratuity depends on completed years of continuous service, and PF is a running account independent of how your notice period was served or bought out.

What happens if I don't serve any notice at all and just stop showing up?

Your employer can withhold your relieving letter, deduct the notice-period equivalent from your final settlement, mark you as "absconded" in some HR systems, and in rare cases pursue legal action — though enforcement varies widely and this can complicate future background checks.

Is a 90-day notice period legal?

Generally yes, if it applies equally to both parties and is proportionate to the seniority of the role. It's a common clause for IT services and senior roles, though it isn't mandated by any statute — it's a negotiated contract term.
